translation:
<column-break/>

Abandoning the high clouds,
the scent of the plum blossoms lingers.
Like the flight of a butterfly,
the tea bowl from the southern fields
is placed there.
<term>Oni</term> <gloss>Demon or Ogre</gloss>

The flowers in the garden are bright,
the many houses in the evening clouds,
the sound of the waves.

The flight of a butterfly,
the hem of the robe is tattered,
I look upon the loquats.

<column-break/>

The clouds over the mountain villa are far away,
the grasses grow thick,
I become drunk and lose my way.
The sound of the mortar,
I am confused and wandering.
The tigers in the mountains,
the path is winding and steep.
The clouds are abandoned,
taking the hands of the fox,
looking at the beauty of the plants.
The moon is dark,
writing on the sleeve,
leaving the morning sun.

LXXV. Verùm baptismus ille Ioannisne planè fuerit an Christi, quaestio est non leuis: Diuorum tamen Athanasij, Cypriani ac Damasceni aliorumque sententia uerior fortè est, qui non Ioannis sed Christi et nostrum dicunt illum fuisse baptismum: quod et alij Graeci ac Latini Patres sacrique Doctores non obscurè ostendunt, dum et multa ibi de nostro baptismo disputant, et baptismum nostrum ibi tunc primum docent institutum.

LXXVI. Et quamuis Augustinus saepè atque alij Christum baptisma Ioannis dicant suscepisse, Ioannis uocant, non quòd ille Ioannis fuerit baptismus, quò reliquus Iudaeorum populus à Ioanne baptizatus est: sed quod à Ioanne is fuerit administratus, nondum Christi et nostro baptismo condito, tunc primum ministerio Ioannis inchoato.

LXXVII. Neque blasphemia haec est, ut cuidam parum cogitanti uisum est, quòd baptismus noster in remissionem detur peccatorum, qua sanè Christus non egebat. Si enim ita licet argumentari, atrocius est quod sequitur: si Christus Ioannis accepit baptismum, qui in poenitentiam erat, qua profectò longè minus Christus indigebat.

<margin>Math. 3.</margin>
LXXVIII. Ridiculum non solum est, sed ualdè impium, quod Lutheranus quidam hic ineptissimè rhetoricatur, Ioannem, dum Christum ad se uenientem prohiberet, dicentem: Ego à te debeo baptizari, et tu uenis ad me? imprudenter et stultè et carnaliter et contumeliosè id fecisse.

LXXIX. Quid his factis, inquit iste, aliud significaret, quàm si disertis uerbis ad Christum diceret: Ego, qui nolo te baptizare, melius et consultius hac de re constitui, quàm tu qui petis baptismum: ego igitur sapiens, tu stultus: ego prudens, tu ineptus.

LXXX. Paulò antè Ioannem Christum fecerant baptizantem, nunc repentè concionatorem quemdam in scenam illum inducunt arrogantem. Haec nimirum est Euangelij huius ratio, ut cum Euangeliorum libro scruta multa lacera et turpissimae sordes extrahamur.

LXXXI. Falsa et illa sunt, quae tamen quasi Euangelicam historiam <term>ὀνειρόγραφοι</term> narrant Magdeburgici, neminem ad baptismum à Ioanne fuisse admissum, nisi peccata sua fuisset prius confessus, et explorasset, an ualedicto Iudaismo, Messiam praesentem fide apprehenderet.

LXXXII. Sed profectò scriptores isti Ioannem sectarium quemdam faciunt praedicantem, qui de speciali illa fide, quae specialior est, quàm species rerum ab Aristotelicis Platoni tributae, uerba multa fecerit, quae tamen inter Lutheri somnia in concauo Lunae nondum erat.
translation:
<margin>Ser. 3. on the goodness of patience, q. 133 to Ant. book 4, chap. 10.</margin>
LXXV. Truly, whether that baptism was John’s or Christ’s is no light question. The opinion of the holy Athanasius, Cyprian, Damascene, and others is perhaps more true, who say it was not John’s, but Christ’s and our baptism. LXXIX. What else would this act signify, he says, than if he said to Christ in explicit words: "I, who do not want to baptize you, have decided this matter better and more wisely than you, who seek baptism: I am therefore wise, you foolish: I am prudent, you inept."

LXXX. A little earlier they had made Christ the one baptizing John, and now they suddenly introduce him onto the stage as an arrogant preacher. This is indeed the method of this Gospel, that with the book of the Gospels we are dragged through many shredded scraps and most filthy trash. LXXXI. Those things are also false, which the Magdeburgians, <term>ὀνειρόγραφοι</term> <gloss>dream-writers</gloss>, narrate as if it were Gospel history: that no one was admitted to baptism by John unless he had first confessed his sins and explored whether, having bid farewell to Judaism, he apprehended the present Messiah by faith. LXXXII. But truly these writers make John a certain sectarian preacher who spoke many words about that special faith, which is more special than the species of things attributed to Plato by the Aristotelians, which, however, among the dreams of Luther, was not yet in the hollow of the Moon.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>without falling into distraction, without letting virtue slip into ordinary speech, and without allowing the teachings to become mere intellectual habit. It is the meeting with the Teacher in the form of the Three Bodies <note>the Dharmakaya, Sambhogakaya, and Nirmanakaya</note>.

The signs and measures of purifying the grasping of appearances and mind are as follows. With the eyes, one attains the unobstructed divine sight, seeing directly through walls and other obstacles as if they were transparent. With the ears, one hears the languages of the six classes of beings, such as gods and <term>nagas</term> <gloss>serpentine spirits</gloss>. With the nose, one smells the fragrances of other pure realms. Because the stains of mental obscurations are purified, unimpeded clairvoyance arises, and one dwells in the exhaustion of contaminated states. Through the purification of grasping at appearances and mind, wisdom seizes its own ground. This is the attainment of the result: the Teacher as the Three Bodies, spontaneously present without effort. This is the sixteenth core instruction. <term>Samaya</term> <gloss>sacred bond</gloss>. <term>Tya tya tya</term> <gloss>seal, seal, seal</gloss. By unifying view, meditation, and conduct, the result of the Three Bodies is delivered to its own place. Thus it is said.

<leaf-break/>

Appearances that have never existed before arise. It is certain that liberation occurs by resolving the artificial duality of Buddhas and sentient beings. For example, just as one sees all four continents from the peak of Mount Meru, the views of all the individual philosophical schools are clearly understood here. One who knows this meaning is called a <term>rtogs ldan</term> <gloss>realized practitioner</gloss>. As for the nature of that realization: for a yogi who realizes this Teacher as the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss>, there is nothing in all of appearance and existence that is not liberated. Having never been deluded, they do not dwell in delusion; delusion is impossible. Having never been a Buddha, they do not dwell in "Buddha"; there is no liberation <note>meaning they are beyond the duality of bondage and liberation</note>. The five poisons have not been abandoned but are self-liberated. Such a person dwells in the state where phenomena are exhausted and the conceptual mind is transcended. Because cyclic existence has become nameless, they are upright. Because the tenets of dualistic phenomena have collapsed, they are spacious within. Because awareness has recognized its own enlightenment, they are at ease. This chapter introduces the yoga of the ultimate view and summarizes its points.

<summary>This page describes the supernatural signs of successful meditation practice and the realization of the non-dual nature of the Buddha and ordinary mind. It emphasizes that a realized practitioner views all phenomena as spontaneously liberated and transcends conventional philosophical tenets.</summary>

The Tutor <term>Seol-seo</term> does not have their months of service counted to reach the Sixth Rank. Junior officials in the Office of Royal Decrees <term>Yemungwan</term> leave their post after one year and two negative performance reviews <term>bu</term>. Officials in the Office of Diplomatic Correspondence <term>Seungmun-won</term> and the National Academy <term>Seonggyun-gwan</term> leave after two negative reviews in summer and one in winter. 

Officials in the Bureau of Books <term>Gyoseo-gwan</term> leave after one year and two negative reviews. 

For the top graduate of the civil exam <term>Tam-hwa-rang</term>, the fifteen months of service are counted from the month they first pay respects to the King. Even if they are not in the top registry during the personnel review, they are promoted to the Sixth Rank. 

For civil officials, service in the posts of Historiographer <term>Geom-yeol</term>, Clerk <term>Sa-rok</term>, Instructor <term>Hun-do</term>, and Inspector <term>Chal-bang</term> is counted by months, not by days, to reach the Sixth Rank after three thousand days <note>This represents roughly 8 years of service</note>. 

For privileged officials <term>Eum</term>, service as a Tutor <term>Geom-gyo</term> or in the Office of Punishment below the rank of high official is counted to reach the Sixth Rank after nine hundred days. Those on the merit list are promoted to the Sixth Rank. If a dismissed official is reinstated, their previous service is counted. 

Service as a Temporary Overseer <term>Ga-gam-yeok</term> is not counted. Once they move to a substantive post, their total service of nine hundred days is counted for promotion to the Sixth Rank. 

Service as a Temporary Ritual Usher <term>Ga-in-ui</term> is not counted. Once they move to a substantive post, their nine hundred days are counted.

### [THE SPHERE OF WATER AND THE CENTER OF THE WORLD. — OPTICS].

<margin>[Continuation of folio 14 recto:] (This is proven by viewing a white line on a black field with two eyes, one of which looks through a <term>blowpipe<note>original: "cier-bottana" (Italian) or "sarbacane" (French); a hollow tube used here as an optical aperture to restrict light.</note></term> and the other through the luminous air).</margin>

THE SURFACE OF THE SPHERE OF WATER ALWAYS BECOMES MORE DISTANT FROM THE CENTER OF THE WORLD —

This occurs because of the terrain carried by the floods of <term>turbid rivers<note>Rivers carrying a high load of suspended sediment or silt.</note></term>, which discharge the soil from their turbulence onto the sea shores and narrow the borders of that sea; furthermore, they raise its bottom, so that by necessity the surface of such an element must rise —

THE CENTER OF THE WORLD ALWAYS SHIFTS ITS POSITION *oppositely* WITHIN THE BODY OF THE EARTH, FLEEING *mo* TOWARD OUR HEMISPHERE —

This is demonstrated by the aforementioned terrain which is continually taken from the shores or the sides of mountains and carried to the seas; the more that is removed from here, the more it lightens, and consequently, the more it becomes heavy where such terrain is discharged by the marine waves; therefore, it is necessary that such a center changes its position.

---

THE SURFACE OF THE SPHERE OF WATER ALWAYS BECOMES MORE DISTANT FROM THE CENTER OF THE WORLD.

This takes place through the lands carried by the overflows of turbid rivers. These discharge the lands that cloud them onto the maritime shores and restrict the shore of the sea; besides this, they raise their bottom, so that by necessity the surface of such an element comes to rise.

THE CENTER OF [OUR] WORLD <note>1. See folio 17 recto.</note> ALWAYS CHANGES PLACE, *opposite to* WITHIN THE BODY OF THE EARTH, FLEEING *mo* TOWARD OUR HEMISPHERE.

This is shown by the aforementioned lands which are continually removed from the beaches [slopes] or sides of the mountains, and carried to the seas; the more that is removed, the more there is a lightening, and consequently, the more there is a weighing down where these lands are discharged by the marine waves; from then on, it is necessary that such a center changes its place.

<note>1. Leonardo is referring to the Earth's center of gravity. As weight (silt and earth) moves from the mountains to the ocean floor, the balance of the planet shifts, causing the geometric center and the gravitational center to move in relation to one another.</note>

## Underground Natural Philosophy. 362

<margin>Salting... the world... with... and... so that... sea...</margin> <note>The marginal note in the original is fragmented and partially illegible.</note> To speak further on this, there is something <term>Mercurialisch</term> <gloss>mercurial</gloss> within salt that is of a burning and acrid nature. Therefore, those who consume far too much salt eventually have to deal with salted humors, <term>die Kräke</term> <gloss>the itch or scabies</gloss>, <term>den Schorbock</term> <gloss>scurvy</gloss>, and finally <term>Aussatz</term> <gloss>leprosy</gloss>, because the use of too much salt causes a body to rot, just as a moderate amount protects it from rotting. We see an example of this in seafaring, where the long-term consumption of salted foods introduces scurvy. And, certainly, here in Bavaria, where the common man salts his food very heavily because of the abundance and cheapness of salt—thinking to protect himself from rot in this way—people fall into heavy, dangerous diseases, especially leprosy. There is a great number of people afflicted with this throughout all of Bavaria. Although some attribute it to pork, which the inhabitants use the most, I blame the excessive use of salt. In other places, people also eat a lot of pork and do not become susceptible to this in the same way. Thus, salt brings great benefit, but no less trouble when it dissolves into a rot. This is not a simple rot, but because of the mixed-in acrimony, it impresses a sharp greed upon the blood and makes everything in the human body acrid, raging within its own frame. And even if salted foods are well sweetened <note>meaning soaked in fresh water to remove the salt</note>, the greater part of the nourishment is nonetheless drawn out with the leached-out salt water

<summary>Becher argues that while moderate salt preserves food, excessive consumption leads to "mercurial" acrimony in the blood, causing scurvy and leprosy, particularly in Bavaria.</summary>

It has been their habit, and the habit of others among the pillars of wisdom—especially the early ones—to provide "reminders" <term>tanbīhāt</term> <gloss>intuitive pointers</gloss> regarding philosophical objectives. These may suffice for the seeker of perfection, even if they are not understood by the people of imagination. 

Others have imagined their pre-existence <term>qidam</term> <gloss>eternity</gloss> without the body. The mentioned proof only negates their pre-existence as abstracted from all bodies. Rather, their existence—not their pre-existence—by way of **transmigration** <term>tanāsukh</term> is not proven by demonstration, as reported from the commentator of *The Intimations*. Perhaps he had a delusion there and did not know that if they were, as they claimed, united in eternity before all bodies, what led them to depart from the **Holy World** <term>‘ālam al-quds</term> and Life—meaning pure abstraction, which is characterized by transcendence over material deficiencies and intellectual life—and to attach to the world of death and darkness—meaning the body, which is subject to natural death and material deficiencies? And who coerced the eternal and imprisoned it by attachment to the personal body, which is like a partner to it? And how was it subjugated to raise the nursing infant, or even the fetus, until it was drawn from the world of holiness and light to its body? 

All of these are persuasive reminders. He pointed to the demonstrative aspect by saying: "How was some of it distinguished from others in eternity?" Its explanation is that if they were eternal, they would either be multiple or one. Both have been shown to be false due to their agreement in species and its concomitants. As he said: "Their species is unified." Likewise for the third possibility, because if that "other" <note>the differentiator</note> were the subject or matter and its accidents, he pointed to its falsehood by saying: "There is no place, neither essentially nor accidentally, nor substrate"—meaning no matter and no subject. And if it were an inherent state within it, he indicated this by saying: "There is neither action nor passion before the body, nor acquired attributes" as occurs after the body—meaning after the attachment to the body is severed. For their individuation through those acquired traits <term>malakāt</term> is, in their view, a truth. Some of the "people of taste" <note>mystics/gnostics</note> said that these...

<margin></margin>
<unclear>state</unclear> within it. And the animal: the souls become individuated after their abstraction; rather, the abstracted lights are absolutely distinguished by the levels specific to them in terms of intensity, weakness, perfection, and deficiency. These do not add to their specific essences except conceptually. For the more intense light is not distinguished from the weaker light except by the specificity of the simple identity. And those acquired identities, if they are made additional to the soul and accidental to it in the knowledge of those specificities, then their individuation is in reality by that identity itself, not by those states that reveal it.
</margin>

<margin></margin>
<unclear>That is</unclear>, since the spirits were pure lights, and luminous things are not distinguished except by intensity, weakness, perfection, and deficiency—as in sensible lights—it must be that the spirits in eternity were distinguished by perfection and deficiency, etc.
</margin>

<margin></margin>
It is not hidden that this does not repel what he mentioned of the falsehood of multiplicity.
</margin>

semper est extra. Cuius hoc indicium est: nam & annulorum eos, qui pala carent, infinitos, homines dicunt, quia semper aliquid est extra sumendū: per similitudinē tamē quandā, & non propriè. Oportet enim & hoc nunquā idē insuper sumi. In circulo verò non ita fit: sed semper quod deinceps sumitur, est solùm aliud. Infinitū igit id est, cuius semper aliquid extrà, ratione quātitatis accipi potest: cuius verò nihil est extra, id est perfectū, ac totū. Hoc. n. pacto totum consueuimus definire, totum dicentes id esse, cuius nil pror-sus abest: vt hominē totū, aut cistellam. Atq. vt quodque, sic & id quod propriè totū est: veluti totū ipsū cuius nihil est extra. Cuius verò aliquid abest, id quicquid abest, vniuersum non est. Totum autem, & perfectum aut idem penitus sunt, aut naturam finitimā habent. Perfectum verò nihil est prorsus, quod non habeat finem. Quocirca putandum est melius Parmenidem Melisso dixisse. Hic enim ipsum infinitum totum appellat: Parmenides autem, totum dicit esse finitum, à medio æquè distans. Fieri enim non potest, vt infinitū cū toto, ac vniuerso, perinde atque cuin lino linum nectatur. Nà hinc & hanc præclarā de infinitò conditionē accipiunt, omnia, inquam, ipsum continere, & vniuersum in se ipso complecti: habet enim similitudinem quandam ad totum. Infinitū enim materiæ perfectionis magnitudinis est, & id, quod est potentia totum, non actu. Est autem diuisibile, ad diminutionem, & ad additionem contrariam, totūmque atque finitum, non per se, sed per aliud: & non continet, sed vt infinitum est, continetur. Quapropter & ignotum est, ea ratione, qua est infinitum. materia nanque formam non habet. Quare patet, partis magis infinitum, quàm totius rationem subire. Materia nanque pars est totius, perinde ac æs, est æneæ statuæ pars. Nam si in rebus sensibilibus continet, & intelligibilibus, etiam ipsum magnum, & paruum cōtinere res intelligibiles oportebat. At absurdum est profectò, ac impossibile, id, quod est ignotum atque indefinitum, continere, ac definire.

### CAPVT VII.
*Quo pacto ex definitione infiniti, assignanda sit ratio eorum quæ de infinito dicuntur.*

Atqui cum ratione etiam fit, vt id quidem, quod in additione cōstitit, nō videatur esse sic infinitū, vt omnē exuperet magnitudine: id verò, quod in diuisione constitit, infinitū esse istiusmodi videatur. Infinitū enim intus perinde atque materia cōtinetur, forma autem continet. Cum ratione etiam accidit, in numero quidē versus minus, minimum esse, finémque: versus autem plus, omnem semper multitudinem exuperare. In magnitudine verò, cōtrarium: versus quidem minus, omnem magnitudinem exuperare: versus autem maius, non esse magnitudinem infinitam. Hæc enim propterea fiunt, quòd ipsum vnum quicquid tādem id sit, indiuisibile est, homo nanque vnus est homo, nō multi. Numerus autem est, vna, plura, quantáve quædam. Quare ad indiuisibile stetur necesse est. duo enim, ac tria, denominatiua nomina sunt: & cæterorum quisque numerorum simili modo. Versus autem plus, fit vt semper intelligatur. Diuisiones enim magnitudinis duas in partes æquales, sunt infinitæ. Quare potentia quidem est, actu non est: sed semper id, quod accipitur, multitudinem omnem exuperat definitam. Sed non est separabilis is numerus diuisionis, nec infinitio permanet: sed fit & quemadmodum tempus, & ipse numerus temporis. In magnitudinibus autem contrarium est. Nam diuiditur quidem in infinita, continuum ipsum: versus autem maius, non est infinitum. quantum enim contingit potentia esse, tantum & actu esse contingit. Quare cùm infinitum nullum sit sensibile corpus, non contingit definitæ magnitudinis omnis exuperationē esse. Alioqui, mauis cælo aliquid erit. Ipsum autem infinitum nō est idem in motu, magnitudine, atque tempore: vt vna quædam natura. Sed posterius dicitur ob prius. Veluti motus quidem dicitur infinitus, quia prius dicitur magnitudo super qua fit motus, & quę alteratur, aut accrescit, tempus autem propter motum. Atque nunc quidem vtimur hisce: posteriùs autem, & quidnam sit horum vnumquodque, & cur omnis magnitudo diuisibilis sit in magnitudines, dicere enitemur. Atqui neque mathematicorum contemplationem ea ratio aufert, quæ infinitum hoc pacto è medio tollit, vt ad incrementum abeat actu sine transitione. Neque enim nunc ipso indigent infinito, neque vtuntur, sed tantam solùm lineam polluant quantum volunt finitam: atque quamuis aliam magnitudinem eadē diuidere ratione, qua diuisa est magnitudo maxima licet. Quare ad ostendendum quidem illo pacto nihil refert prorsus: esse autem ipsum in his est magnitudinibus, quæ in rerum sunt ratione. Cùm verò causæ in quatuor sint distinctæ, patet, infinitum vt materiam causam esse, & esse quidem ipsius priuationem esse: per se autem subiectum, continuum ipsum atque sensibile esse. Cæteri etiam omnes ipso infinito vt materia vti videntur. Quapropter & absurdum est sanè, ipsum id esse quod continet, & nō id quod continetur, asserere.

### Κεφάλαιον ζ'.
*Πῶς χρὴ ἐκ τοῦ ὁρισμοῦ τοῦ ἀπείρου λόγον ποιεῖσθαι τῶν αἰεὶ ἀπειρουμένων.*

Κατὰ λόγον δὲ συμβαίνει καὶ τὸ κατὰ πρόσθεσιν, ὡς μὴ δοκεῖν ἄπειρον οὕτως, ὥστε παντὸς ὑπερβάλλειν τὸ μέγεθος· ἐπὶ τὴν διαίρεσιν δὲ, ὑπερβάλλειν. καὶ γὰρ ὡς ἡ ὕλη ἐντὸς, καὶ τὸ ἄπειρον· περιέχει δὲ τὸ εἶδος. εὐλόγως δὲ καὶ τὸ, ἐν μὲν τῷ ἀριθμῷ ἐπὶ τὸ ἐλάχιστον πέρας· ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ πλεῖον, αἰεὶ παντὸς ὑπερβάλλειν πλήθους· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν μεγεθῶν τοὐναντίον· ἐπὶ μὲν τὸ ἔλαττον, παντὸς ὑπερβάλλειν μεγέθους· ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ μεῖζον, μὴ εἶναι μέγεθος ἄπειρον. αἴτιον δ’, ὅτι τὸ ἕν ἐστιν ἀδιαίρετον, ὅπερ ἂν ᾖ, οἷον ἄνθρωπος εἷς ἄνθρωπος, καὶ οὐ πολλοί· ὁ δ’ ἀριθμός ἐστιν ἕνα πλείω, καὶ ποσὰ ἄττα· ὥστ’ ἀνάγκη στῆναι ἐπὶ τὸ ἀδιαίρετον· τὰ γὰρ δύο καὶ τρία παρώνυμα ὀνόματά ἐστιν, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἀριθμῶν ἕκαστος· ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ πλεῖον αἰεὶ ἔστι νοῆσαι· ἄπειροι γὰρ αἱ διχοτομίαι τοῦ μεγέθους· ὥστε δυνάμει μὲν ἔστιν, ἐνεργείᾳ δ’ οὔ· ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ ὑπερβάλλει τὸ λαμβανόμενον, παντὸς ὡρισμένου πλήθους· ἀλλ’ οὐ χωριστὸς ὁ ἀριθμὸς οὗτος τῆς διχοτομίας, οὐδὲ μένει ἡ ἀπειρία, ἀλλὰ γίνεται, ὥσπερ καὶ ὁ χρόνος καὶ ὁ ἀριθμὸς τοῦ χρόνου. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν μεγεθῶν, τοὐναντίον ἐστίν· καὶ διαιρεῖται μὲν γὰρ εἰς ἄπειρα τὸ συνεχές. ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ μεῖζον οὐκ ἔστιν ἄπειρον. ὅσον γὰρ ἐνδέχεται δυνάμει εἶναι, καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ ἐνδέχεται τοσοῦτον εἶναι. ὥστ’ ἐπεὶ ἄπειρον οὐδέν ἐστι μέγεθος αἰσθητὸν, οὐκ ἐνδέχεται παντὸς ὑπερβολὴν εἶναι ὡρισμένου μεγέθους· εἴη γὰρ ἄν τι τοῦ οὐρανοῦ μεῖζον. τὸ δ’ ἄπειρον, οὐ ταὐτὸν ἐν κινήσει, καὶ μεγέθει, καὶ χρόνῳ, ὡς καὶ μία τις φύσις, ἀλλὰ τὸ ὕστερον λέγεται κατὰ τὸ πρότερον· οἷον, κίνησις μὲν, ὅτι τὸ μέγεθος, ἐφ’ οὗ κινεῖται, ἢ ἀλλοιοῦται, ἢ αὐξάνεται, ὁ χρόνος δὲ διὰ τὴν κίνησιν. νῦν μὲν οὖν χρώμεθα τούτοις, ὕστερον δ’ ἐροῦμεν τί ἐστιν ἕκαστον, καὶ διότι πᾶν μέγεθος εἰς μεγέθη διαιρετόν. Οὐκ ἀφαιρεῖται δὲ ὁ λόγος οὐδὲ τοὺς μαθηματικοὺς τὴν θεωρίαν, ἀναιρῶν οὕτως εἶναι τὸ ἄπειρον, ὡς ἐνεργείᾳ εἶναι ἐπὶ τὴν αὔξησιν, ὡς ἀδιεξίτητον· οὐδὲ γὰρ νῦν δέονται τοῦ ἀπείρου, οὐδὲ χρῶνται, ἀλλὰ μόνον εἶναι, ὅσην ἂν βούλωνται, πεπερασμένην· τῷ δὲ μεγίστῳ μεγέθει τὸν αὐτὸν ἔστι τετμῆσθαι λόγον ὁπηλικονοῦν μέγεθος ἕτερον. ὥστε πρὸς μὲν τὸ δεῖξαι ἐκείνοις, οὐδὲν διοίσει τὸ εἶναι ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν ἔστη μεγέθεσιν. ἐπεὶ δὲ τὰ αἴτια διῄρηται τέσσαρα, φανερὸν ὅτι τὸ ἄπειρον αἴτιόν ἐστι καὶ ὅτι, τὸ μὲν εἶναι αὐτῷ στέρησίς ἐστι, τὸ δὲ καθ’ αὑτὸ ὑποκείμενον, τὸ συνεχὲς καὶ αἰσθητόν. φαίνονται δὲ πάντες καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι ὡς ὕλῃ χρώμενοι τῷ ἀπείρῳ· διὸ καὶ ἄτοπον τὸ περιέχον ποιεῖν αὐτὸ, ἀλλὰ μὴ τὸ περιεχόμενον.

The proof of this is as follows: for people say that even rings which lack a bezel are infinite, because there is always something outside to be taken: though this is by a certain similarity, and not properly. For it is necessary that this same thing is never taken over and above. In a circle, however, this does not happen: but what is taken next is always merely another thing. The <term>infinitum</term> <gloss>infinite</gloss> is, therefore, that which, in terms of quantity, always has something outside that can be taken: but that which has nothing outside it, is perfect and whole. For in this manner we are accustomed to define the whole, calling that a whole from which nothing at all is missing: as a whole man, or a whole basket. And as it is with each thing, so it is with that which is properly whole: such as the whole itself, of which nothing is outside. But if anything is missing from it, then whatever is missing means it is not a universe. The whole and the perfect are either entirely the same, or have a nature bordering upon one another. Nothing is perfect, however, which does not have an end. Wherefore it must be thought that Parmenides spoke better than Melissus. For the latter calls the infinite itself a whole; Parmenides, however, says the whole is finite, equidistant from the center. For it cannot happen that the infinite is joined to the whole and the universe, just as one thread is joined to another. From this, indeed, they receive this noble condition regarding the infinite, namely, that it contains all things, and embraces the universe within itself: for it has a certain similarity to the whole. For the infinite is the matter of the perfection of magnitude, and it is a whole in potentiality, but not in actuality. It is divisible, toward diminution and toward the opposite, addition, and it is a whole and finite, not of itself, but through another: and it does not contain, but insofar as it is infinite, it is contained. Wherefore it is also unknown, for the reason that it is infinite. For matter has no form. Wherefore it is clear that the infinite is subject to the reason of a part rather than a whole. For matter is a part of the whole, just as bronze is a part of a bronze statue. For if it contains in sensible and intelligible things, it ought also to contain intelligible things within the great and the small. But it is absurd, indeed, and impossible, that that which is unknown and indefinite should contain and define.

### CHAPTER VII.
*How, from the definition of the infinite, the account of those things which are said about the infinite is to be assigned.*

And yet, it happens with reason that that which consists in addition does not seem to be infinite in such a way that it surpasses every magnitude: but that which consists in division seems to be infinite in this way. For the infinite is contained within just as matter is, while form contains. It also happens with reason that, in number, toward the less, there is a minimum and an end: but toward the more, it always surpasses every multitude. In magnitude, however, the opposite occurs: toward the less, it surpasses every magnitude: but toward the greater, there is no infinite magnitude. These things happen because the one, whatever it may be, is indivisible; for one man is a man, not many. Number, however, is one, many, and certain quantities. Wherefore it is necessary to stand upon the indivisible. For two and three are denominative names: and each of the other numbers in a similar way. But toward the more, it happens that it can always be understood. For divisions of a magnitude into two parts are infinite. Wherefore it is in potentiality, but not in actuality: but that which is taken always surpasses every defined multitude. But this number of division is not separable, nor does the infinity remain: but it comes to be just like time and the number of time. In magnitudes, however, the opposite is true. For the continuous itself is indeed divided into infinite parts: but toward the greater, it is not infinite. For as much as it happens to be in potentiality, it also happens to be in actuality. Wherefore, since no sensible body is infinite, it does not happen that there is an excess over every defined magnitude. Otherwise, something would be greater than the heavens. The infinite itself is not the same in motion, magnitude, and time, as if it were one certain nature. But the later is said because of the earlier. Just as motion is called infinite because the magnitude over which it occurs, and which is altered or grows, is called so first, and time is called so because of the motion. And now indeed we are using these terms: but later we shall endeavor to say what each of these is, and why every magnitude is divisible into magnitudes. Nor does this account remove the contemplation of the mathematicians, which destroys the infinite in this way, so that it might go toward increment in actuality without transition. For they do not need the infinite now, nor do they use it, but they only postulate a line as finite as they wish: and it is permitted to divide any other magnitude by the same reason by which the largest magnitude is divided. Wherefore, in order to demonstrate that, it makes no difference at all that it exists among these magnitudes which are in the realm of reason. Since causes are distinguished into four, it is clear that the infinite is a cause as matter, and that its being is a privation: but the subject in itself is the continuous and sensible. All others also seem to use the infinite itself as matter. Wherefore it is also absurd, indeed, to assert that it is that which contains, and not that which is contained.

<column-break/>

And because outside, but that of which there is always something outside, this is infinite. A sign of this is that they even say that rings which do not have a bezel are infinite, because there is always something outside to take, speaking by a certain similarity, but not properly; for it is necessary that this should exist in this way, and that the same thing should never be taken. But in a circle, this does not happen, but the next thing is always merely another. Therefore, the infinite is that of which, as we take it according to quantity, there is always something outside to take. And that of which there is nothing outside, that is perfect and whole; for thus we define the whole, of which nothing is absent, such as a whole man or a whole chest. And as it is with each thing, so it is with that which is properly so; such as the whole, of which nothing is outside; but that from which something is outside, is not all, whatever is absent. The whole and the perfect are either entirely the same or near to each other in nature. Nothing is perfect that does not have an end; and the end is a boundary. Therefore, one must think that Parmenides spoke better than Melissus; for the former says the infinite is the whole; the latter, that the whole is bounded,

for he would not join thread to thread to the universe and the whole, regarding the infinite; since from this they receive the majesty regarding the infinite, that it contains all things, and has the universe within itself, because it has a certain similarity to the whole; for the infinite is the matter of the perfection of magnitude, and it is a whole in potentiality, but not in actuality; and it is divisible, regarding the process of diminution and the reversed process of addition; but it is a whole and finite, not of itself, but according to another; and it does not contain, but is contained, insofar as it is infinite; wherefore it is also unknown, insofar as it is infinite. Parmenides said "the whole" [in these words]: "All things equal to the bulk of a sphere. Equidistant from the center everywhere."

### CHAPTER VII.
*How one must make an account of those things that are always being infinitized from the definition of the infinite.*

It happens with reason that even that which is according to addition does not seem to be infinite in such a way as to surpass every magnitude; but toward division, it does surpass. For as matter is within, so is the infinite; but form contains. It happens reasonably that in number there is a limit toward the least; but toward the more, it always surpasses every multitude; but in magnitudes, the opposite is true; toward the less, it surpasses every magnitude; but toward the greater, there is no infinite magnitude. The cause is that the one is indivisible, whatever it may be, such as one man is one man, and not many; but number is more than one, and certain quantities; so it is necessary to stop at the indivisible; for two and three are denominative names, and in the same way, each of the other numbers; but toward the more, it is always possible to think; for the divisions of a magnitude are infinite; so it is in potentiality, but not in actuality; but the thing taken always surpasses every defined multitude; but this number of division is not separable, nor does the infinity remain, but it comes to be, just as time and the number of time. But in magnitudes, the opposite is true; for the continuous is divided into infinite parts. But toward the greater, it is not infinite. For as much as it is possible to be in potentiality, so much is it possible to be in actuality. So since no sensible magnitude is infinite, it is not possible for there to be an excess over every defined magnitude; for there would be something larger than the heavens. But the infinite is not the same in motion, and magnitude, and time, as if it were one certain nature, but the later is said according to the former; as, motion is [infinite], because the magnitude over which it moves, or is altered, or grows, [is so], and time [is so] because of the motion. Now we are using these, but later we shall say what each is, and why every magnitude is divisible into magnitudes. Nor does the account remove the contemplation of the mathematicians, destroying the infinite in such a way that it is in actuality toward increase, as if it were untraversable; for they do not need the infinite now, nor do they use it, but only [require it] to be finite, as much as they wish; and it is possible to cut the same proportion upon the largest magnitude with another magnitude of any size. So, regarding proving those things to them, it will make no difference that it exists among the existing magnitudes. And since causes are divided into four, it is clear that the infinite is a cause, and that its being is a privation, but the subject in itself is the continuous and sensible. And all others seem to use the infinite as matter; wherefore it is absurd to make it the container, and not the contained.
